text: Did you hear that? The map just came loose. I’m holding the file… it’s heavy. Before we open it, watch how I’d finish a “because” line about a different place: “People in my town built a big bridge because the river is too wide to swim.” The land had something, so people did something. Pause me and finish one of yours that way. … Got one? Good. Now the file.

This next voice is reading real words from about 450 years ago. A Spanish boy named Fontaneda was shipwrecked in Florida and lived with the people here for seventeen years. Later he wrote down what he saw. Listen for a season hiding in his words.

“They have bread of roots, which is their common food the greater part of the time… Because of the lake, which rises in some seasons so high that the roots cannot be reached in consequence of the water, they are for some time without eating this bread.”
Pause me. Which season made the lake rise? And what would people have to do when they couldn’t reach their roots? … Got an idea? Check it against the wheel.
You did it! This file is finished.
The land decided a lot. People farmed where there was good soil and rain. They fished where there was water. The seasons worked the same way. You’ll see that in tab 2.
I found today’s file. It’s called First Peoples. But it’s locked, and a map of Florida is stuck on the front.
To open it, you’ll match four clues to the right places on the Florida map. The map is in the Map Quest tab, below the welcome video. I can’t reach it from in here, but you can.
In a new room! I can hear seagulls and smell salt water. I think one of the next files is about explorers and their ships.

Now for the writing. In the Historian’s Notebook tab (tab 4), you’ll pick one season and one group of people. Then you’ll write about one day in their life, as if you were there. Use the planner first. It helps you choose what to write about.
Bye! Don’t forget to copy or download your work and turn it in on Canvas. I’ll text you when the next file shows up.
Go to the Source Study tab (tab 2). Open the four season files and read them. Then put each card on the right part of the year-wheel.
I’m okay, just a little dusty. Every file you finish gets me one room closer to getting out. So let’s start with the map!
Where do you want to start?
It’s about one year in the life of Florida’s first peoples, one season at a time. You’ll read it in the Source Study tab after the map is done.
Scroll down past the welcome video. Drag each clue onto the place in Florida where it fits. If a clue bounces back, read the hint and try a different place.
You did it! All four clues are in the right places, and the map let go of the file. Before you move on, finish the “because” sentences under the map. You’ll use them in Evidence Question 1.
Answer from what you just read. If you’re not sure, look back at the season files.
Nice work! All four cards are on the right seasons. It’s the same village, but life looks very different in each season. Next is the Self-Check tab (tab 3): three quick questions.
That’s okay. The check isn’t graded. If you miss one, reread that season before you start writing.

Here’s how I’d start a Day in the Life, but about my own day, so I’m not doing yours: “The rain was already loud on the roof when I woke up, so I knew the drive would be slow.” Hear it? A weather detail, then what it made me do. That’s the trick. Pause me and write your first sentence that way, for your people and your season. … Done? Keep going, and don’t skip the hard part. Real days have one.

From in here I can see your reminder card, and right now it’s blank. Before you fill it in, think about the last time someone got your name wrong. Maybe a substitute, or a relative who mixed you up with your cousin. It’s a small thing, but you noticed. Now picture a whole group of people called by the wrong name for five hundred years. That’s where the first habit comes from. When you write each habit on the card, use words you’d use with a younger cousin.

From the Constitution of the Seminole Tribe of Florida, 1957. “We, the members of the Seminole Tribe of Florida, in order to promote justice, insure tranquility, encourage the general welfare, safeguard our interests and secure the blessings of freedom and liberty for ourselves and for our posterity, do hereby form and organize a Seminole Tribal Council…”

That was the start of the Constitution of the Seminole Tribe of Florida. The Seminole people wrote it and voted on it in 1957, and their government still uses it today. Did you catch the word “posterity”? It means the children and grandchildren who come later. That’s the same idea as descendants. Notice who’s talking, too. This isn’t someone from far away describing them. It’s the tribe writing about itself. Open the habit files and find the one this document fits best.

Remember the old textbook sentence you’re about to fix? I found that book on a shelf in the room I’m stuck in. Before you start, I’ll fix a different sentence out loud, mistakes and all. “Pioneers in Florida lived hard lives.” Hmm. Which pioneers? “Cattle ranchers in Florida lived hard lives.” Better. But hard how? “In the 1800s, Florida cattle ranchers rode for days to drive their cows to ships on the Gulf coast.” Now I can see them. It took me three tries, and that’s normal. Use your planner, and expect to change your sentence at least once.
You did it! This file is finished.

Now for the writing. In the Historian’s Notebook tab (tab 4), you’ll answer three questions. Then you’ll fix a careless sentence from an old textbook. Use the planner first. It helps you choose what to put in.
This file is about how we write about real people, so we tell their story the right way.
Nice work! You found every detail. Same people, but one sentence shows them clearly and the other doesn’t. Next is the Self-Check tab (tab 3): three quick questions.
Answer from what you just read. If you’re not sure, look back at the habit files.
You did it! All four habits are on your card, and the file let go. Keep your card in mind. It can help you with Evidence Question 1.
Bye! Don’t forget to copy or download your work and turn it in on Canvas. I’ll text you when the next file shows up.
That’s okay. The check isn’t graded. If you miss one, reread that habit file before you start writing.
Where do you want to start?
A habit is something you do every time, without anyone telling you. These four are things careful historians do every time they write about real people.
To open it, you’ll make a reminder card. Match each of four habits to the example that shows it. Then write each habit in your own words. The card is in the Make a Card tab, below the welcome video.
I’m okay. Every file you finish gets me one room closer to getting out. This is the last file in this part, so let’s finish it well!
The way we write about people changes what readers think of them. In tab 2 you’ll see two sentences about the same people. They leave very different pictures.
In a new room! I can hear the ocean, and I can see tall wooden ships far away. I think the next file is about explorers.
Go to the Source Study tab (tab 2). Open the four habit files and read them. Then find the details the careless sentence left out.
Scroll down past the welcome video. Drag each habit onto the example that shows it, or tap a habit and then tap the example. Then write that habit in your own words.

Did you hear that? The ships clicked into place, and the route file came loose. From in here I can see all three: the small one, the bigger one, and the biggest. But here’s what I keep looking at. Every ship landed on a shore where people already lived. When you get to the Source Study tab, watch for the people on the shore, not just the ships.

Before you write, I’ll try one out loud about something different. “In 2019, the Parker family moved onto my street. For the kids who already lived there, it meant a new friend. It also meant sharing the basketball hoop.” See what I put in? A name, a year, and what it meant for the people already there, the good and the hard. Now it’s your turn with the explorers. Use your planner.
You did it! This file is finished.
You did it! All three ships are in order: 1513, 1528, 1539. The file let go. Keep those years handy. You’ll need them for Evidence Question 1.
To open it, put three ships in order on a timeline. The timeline is in the Route File tab, below the welcome video.

Go to the Source Study tab (tab 2). Put each explorer’s ship where he landed on the map, then read his part of the story. After that, study the old Spanish map and match each ship to what it meant for the people on the shore.

Now for the writing. In the Historian’s Notebook tab (tab 4), answer three questions. Then write 3 to 5 sentences about who came to Florida and what it meant for the people already living here. Use the planner first.
In a new room! There’s an old desk in here covered in papers with Spanish writing on them. I think the next file is about why the Spanish came at all.
Scroll down past the welcome video. Drag each ship onto its year, or tap a ship and then tap the year. Read the clue on each ship. It tells you which one came first.
Bye! Don’t forget to copy or download your work and turn it in on Canvas. I’ll text you when the next file shows up.
Go to the Self-Check tab (tab 3). Answer from what you just read. If you’re not sure, look back at the timeline.
Putting events in order helps historians see how one thing led to another. You’ll use these years in your writing, too.
Where do you want to start?
I’m okay. Every file you finish gets me one room closer to getting out. I can hear waves in this room!
Nice work! Every ship is matched to the shore. Remember, people lived on that shore the whole time. Next is the Self-Check tab (tab 3): three quick questions.
An explorer is someone who travels to a place that’s new to them, to learn about it or claim it (say it belongs to their country). These explorers sailed for Spain.
That’s okay. The check isn’t graded. If you miss one, reread that part of the story before you start writing.
This file is about the first Spanish explorers who came to Florida, and the people who were already here.
That’s a promise inside the deal: the title of admiral. It tells what Columbus would get, not who gave the order. Try another number.
That’s a promise inside the deal: gold and silver. It tells what Columbus would get, not who gave the order. Try another number.

I’m looking at the chart from in here, and it’s still blank. The title says Why They Sailed, but every row is empty. Every card you pack tells me why those ships kept coming. Start with the one you’re surest about.

Did you hear that? Click, click, click. All three trunks just locked. Now look at them. Which one is heaviest? Hold on to your answer. In the Source Study tab, you’ll see which reasons the Spanish actually wrote into their deals.
Before you read, pause me. Why would you sail across an ocean you’d never seen? Pick one reason. Just one. Got it? Keep it in mind. You’ll find out if the Spanish picked the same one.

Here’s how I figure out what kind of paper something is. Yesterday I got three things in the mail. A birthday card signed “Love, Aunt Rose.” A bill with a company’s name at the top. And a notice from school that said “by order of the principal.” The signature and those words told me who it was from. Now tap the gold numbers and do the same thing.

Before you fill the scale, I’ll weigh one of mine. Once I drove three hours in a storm to get to a friend’s wedding. What did it take? Courage, and a long, scary drive. What did it cost? My family worried, and I missed my nephew’s game. Was it wise? Partly. See how both sides count? Now try it with the explorers.
Here’s a Spanish soldier named Bernal Díaz. He sailed to Mexico, not Florida. He wrote this as an old man, about his friends who had died there. Listen for the three G’s.
…who rendered such important services to God and to their emperor, and who gave light to those who lived in darkness… They did not even obtain wealth, although this is the goal of all men!

Did you hear God? Did you hear gold, the wealth? “Their emperor” was the king of Spain, and serving him was Glory. And notice he called the Native people “those who lived in darkness.” That’s how he saw them. They had their own beliefs. Pause me and pick the G you think he cared about most.
You did it! This file is finished.
This file is about why Spain kept sending ships to Florida. There were three big reasons: God, Gold, and Glory.
I’m okay. Every file you finish gets me one room closer to getting out. This room smells like old paper!
Nice work! You proved it: it’s an order from the king and queen, and it promised Columbus a title and treasure. Next is the Self-Check tab (tab 3).
You did it! All three trunks are packed, and the file let go. Keep God, Gold, and Glory in your head. You’ll use them in every question today.
To open it, pack three expedition trunks. Each detail goes in the trunk for its reason. The trunks are in the Pack the Trunks tab, below the welcome video.
Go to the Self-Check tab (tab 3). Three quick questions. If you’re not sure, look back at the reading.

Now for the writing. In the Historian’s Notebook tab (tab 4), answer three questions. Then write 4 to 6 sentences about what Spain hoped to gain, and whether their courage was used wisely. Fill in the courage scale first.
In a new room! There are three flags on the wall: Spain’s, France’s, and England’s. I think the next file is about who wanted Florida.
That’s okay. The check isn’t graded. If you miss one, reread that part before you start writing.
Bye! Don’t forget to copy or download your work and turn it in on Canvas. I’ll text you when the next file shows up.
Where do you want to start?
Glory means honor and rewards, like a special title (a name of honor, such as Admiral) or land of your own. Explorers wanted them, and so did Spain.
Good question to keep asking. In the Source Study tab, you’ll see which reasons the Spanish actually wrote into their deals.
Scroll down past the welcome video. Drag each detail card into a trunk, or tap a card and then tap a trunk.
Go to the Source Study tab (tab 2). Read about God, Gold, and Glory one part at a time. Then look at a real agreement from 1492 and figure out what kind of document it is.

I’m standing under three flags in here, and they all point at the same coast: Spain, France, and England. Before you plant them, look at the map. See how close Fort Caroline and St. Augustine are? About thirty-five miles. Close enough for soldiers to march there in a few days. Keep that in mind.

Look at the glow where the claims touch. That’s the trouble spot. Two countries, one small piece of coast. When two people want the same thing, what usually happens? Hold on to your answer. In the Explore tab, you’ll see what really happened.

Here’s a domino chain from my own life. My alarm didn’t go off, so I woke up late. I woke up late, so I missed the bus. I missed the bus, so I was late to school. Each one caused the next. Now look at your dominoes. For each one, ask: what made this happen?

Before you fill the ledger, I’ll try one column: France. Motive? The Huguenots wanted a safe place to practice their faith. That’s God. Event? They built Fort Caroline in 1564. One motive, one event. Now you try all three columns. And don’t forget the people who were already here.
Here’s René de Laudonnière. He was the French captain who built Fort Caroline in 1564. He climbed a hill by the St. Johns River and wrote about what he saw. Listen for why the French wanted to stay.

Therefore I went right to the top thereof, where we found nothing else but cedars, palm, and bay trees of so sovereign odour, that balm smelleth nothing like in comparison… Briefly, the place is so pleasant, that those which are melancholic would be enforced to change their humour.

Did you catch that? Melancholic means sad. He said this place was so pleasant that even a sad person would cheer up. The French wanted to stay. So did Spain. And the Timucua already lived there. Pause me and think: what happens when everyone wants the same place?
You did it! This file is finished.
Good question. The year slider in the Explore tab shows you, one year at a time.
In a new room! There’s a big chart on the wall with two columns: Causes and Effects. I think the next file is about what all this changed for Florida.
You did it! All three flags are on the coast. See where the claims overlap? That glow is where the trouble started.
Scroll down past the welcome video. Drag each flag card to its spot on the map, or tap a card and then tap a spot.
Nice work! Both lines of dominoes fell. One event led to the next. Next is the Self-Check tab (tab 3).
Go to the Self-Check tab (tab 3). Three quick questions. If you’re not sure, look back at the year slider.
That’s okay. The check isn’t graded. If you miss one, reread that part before you start writing.
Bye! Don’t forget to copy or download your work and turn it in on Canvas. I’ll text you when the next file shows up.
This file is about three countries that all wanted Florida: Spain, France, and England.

Now for the writing. In the Historian’s Notebook tab (tab 4), answer three questions. Then write 4 to 6 sentences about why three countries fought over Florida, and what it meant for the people already here. Fill in the three-flag ledger first.
Go to the Explore tab (tab 2). Slide through the years and watch the map change. Then line up the dominoes to show what caused what.
Where do you want to start?
To open it, plant each country’s flag where it came to Florida’s coast. The map is in the Claim the Coast tab, below the welcome video.
Huguenots were French Protestants, a kind of Christian. In France they were often treated badly for their faith, so some hoped Florida could be a safe home.
I’m okay. The flags on this wall keep moving, like there’s a breeze. Every file you finish gets me one room closer to the door!

Here’s a string board from my own life. Cause: I forgot to water my garden for a week. Effect: my tomato plants wilted. Another cause: it rained all weekend. Effect: my soccer game got canceled. One string for each. Now look at your board. For each cause, ask: what did this lead to?

Look at your strings. Some causes were choices people made, like building a fort. One cause, sickness, wasn’t a choice at all. Nobody back then knew about germs. But its effect was the biggest of all. Keep that in mind when you read the next part.

Here’s how I’d read the growth chart on my kitchen door frame. It says: Sam, four feet tall, May 2025. I can infer Sam grew, because last year’s mark is lower. But I still have to ask: why did Sam grow so fast this year? The chart can’t tell me. Now try the same three questions on the baptism book.

Here’s a chain from my own life. Cause: our town built a new park. Effect: more families walk there on weekends. Evidence: the sign-in sheet at the gate has more names each month. Lens: building it took hard work, and it cost a few old trees. Now build your chain. Four links, and don’t skip one.

In 1707, the priests in St. Augustine wrote a letter to the king of Spain about what had happened to the Apalachee missions. Here is a short part, in English. Listen for two reasons the mission towns were emptying.

…very depopulated on account of the many plagues and sicknesses that have consumed them… many others of the said province, and of Timucua and Guale, have been sold and have passed to the islands of the domain of the Queen of England.

Depopulated means emptied of people. Plagues and sicknesses are diseases. Sold to the islands means people were captured and sold as slaves on English islands in the Caribbean Sea. Pause me and say the two reasons out loud.
You did it! This file is finished.
Go to the Explore tab (tab 2). Tap the ship to send out ripples and read each part. Then sort the cards about the baptism book.
Out of the Unit 4 room! The next room is a big hall with all four Florida Files on the walls. Next time we put them all together.
Now for the writing. In the Historian’s Notebook tab (tab 4), answer three questions. Then write 5 to 7 sentences about the causes and effects of colonization. Build the cause-and-effect chain first.
Scroll down past the welcome video. Tap a cause on the left, then tap the effect it led to. Or drag the cause card onto its effect.
Because effects keep spreading, like rings on water. Some effects from 400 years ago are still part of Florida today.
To open it, tie strings from causes to effects. The String Board is in the String Board tab, below the welcome video.
A cause is what makes something happen. An effect is what happens because of it. Rain is a cause. A wet sidewalk is an effect.
Go to the Self-Check tab (tab 3). Three quick questions. If you’re not sure, look back at the ripples.
Bye! Don’t forget to copy or download your work and turn it in on Canvas. I’ll text you when the next file shows up.
You did it! Every string is tied. See how one cause can lead to something big? Next is the Explore tab (tab 2).
This is the last file of Unit 4. It’s about what colonization caused in Florida. Colonization is when a country sends people to take over land far away and rule it.
Where do you want to start?
I’m okay. The chart on this wall has strings hanging loose. I think if you tie them, the last door in this unit will open!
Nice work! You sent every ripple and sorted every card. Next is the Self-Check tab (tab 3).
To infer is to figure something out from clues. The book doesn’t say it in words, but the clues point to it.

Here’s how I sorted my junk drawer at home. I made three piles: things for the kitchen, things for school, and things to fix. A dead flashlight went in the fix pile. A pencil went in the school pile. My one rule: ask what the thing is about, then pick its pile. Now try that with each card.

Look at your drawers. You studied the land in Unit 2, the First Peoples in Unit 3, and the explorers in Unit 4. Three different units. But they aren’t three different stories. In the Explore tab, you’ll see how they connect into one.

Here’s the whole chain in one breath. The land came first. The land shaped where the First Peoples lived. Then ships came from Europe looking for gold and land. And contact changed everything for the people already here. Pause me and say the chain back, out loud, in your own words.

Here’s an honest check from my own life. My sister says our corner shop has the best pizza in the whole world. Did she taste every pizza in the world? No. That’s stretching. Honest would be: it’s the best pizza I’ve ever had. Now check each sentence. Does it say more than the cards show? Does it leave someone out?

Here’s a bridge from my own life. Post one: my street got a new stop sign. Post two: cars slowed down at the corner. Post three: kids can walk to school safely. Now the planks. We got a stop sign, so cars slowed down. Cars slowed down, and this meant kids could walk safely. Now build yours. Three posts, and a plank in every gap.
You did it! This file is finished.
Start with the file drawers in the File Drawers tab, below the welcome video.
Go to the Explore tab (tab 2). Build the map one layer at a time and read each part. Then sort the sentences into trays.
Now for the writing. In the Historian’s Notebook tab (tab 4), answer three questions. Then write 4 to 5 sentences that connect three cards. Build the bridge first.
Because you can’t connect things until you know what you have. Sorting comes first. Connecting comes next.
A long hallway, and another door at the end. It’s not the way out yet, but I’m closer than ever. Next time we answer one big question: what changed after contact?
You did it! Every card is in its drawer. Next is the Explore tab (tab 2).
Nice work! The map is built and every sentence is sorted. Next is the Self-Check tab (tab 3).
Go to the Self-Check tab (tab 3). Three quick questions. If you’re not sure, look back at the map.
Three drawers: Florida’s land and water, the First Peoples, and the explorers. You studied them in Units 2, 3, and 4.
A checkpoint is a stop where you have to show what you know before you can go on. The sign on this door says: Sort the first Florida files, then connect them.
Stretching the evidence means saying more than the facts show. If the cards say some people fought back, you can’t say everyone was happy.
Where do you want to start?
Scroll down past the welcome video. Tap a card, then tap the drawer it belongs in. Or drag the card onto the drawer.
Bye! Don’t forget to copy or download your work and turn it in on Canvas. I’ll text you when I reach the next door.
I hope so! I can see light around the edges of the door. Let’s find out together.

Here’s a two-sided card from my own life. When our town built a new highway, we got places faster. That’s what arrived. But the old farm by the road was torn down. That’s who paid. Both are true. Now put each fact on its side of the council card.

Look at your card. Imagine if it had only one side, just what arrived. It would sound cheerful, but it would leave people out. That’s why the council wants both. Next, in the Explore tab, you’ll hear both sides out loud.

You just heard two voices at one table. Pause me and try this. Say one thing that arrived in Florida. Then say one thing the First Peoples lost. Say them together in one breath, with the words even as in the middle.

Here’s a sentence about my school: We got new computers this year. True! But it’s only half. Here’s the whole one: We got new computers this year, even as our art class was cut. Now check each sentence. Does it have both halves?

Here’s how I fill both hands. Left hand: our library got new books. Right hand: the reading corner lost its comfy chairs to make room. Joining words: even as. Why both? Because both are true, and the kids who loved those chairs count too. Now fill your hands. Don’t leave one empty.
You did it! This file is finished.
Not yet, I think. But it’s the last gate of this checkpoint. Let’s open it.
Now for the writing. In the Historian’s Notebook tab (tab 4), answer three questions. Then write your Council Debrief in 4 to 5 sentences. Fill both hands first.
A whole sentence names what arrived AND who paid. If one half is missing, it’s only half the story.
A brand-new hallway, with a sign: St. Augustine. The next files are about Spanish Florida and its missions.
Contact is the time when Europeans and the First Peoples first met. A lot changed after that, for both sides.
You did it! Both sides of the card are full. Next is the Explore tab (tab 2).
Scroll down past the welcome video. Tap a fact, then tap the side of the card it belongs on. Or drag it.
Bye! Don’t forget to copy or download your work and turn it in on Canvas. I’ll text you from the next hallway.
Nice work! You heard both voices and checked every sentence. Next is the Self-Check tab (tab 3).
Start with the council card in the Council Card tab, below the welcome video.
Go to the Explore tab (tab 2). Tap the seats at the council table to hear both perspectives. Then check which sentences are whole.
Where do you want to start?
Go to the Self-Check tab (tab 3). Three quick questions. If you’re not sure, listen to the two voices again.
Because both things happened at the same time, to different people. Leaving one out isn’t honest.
A council is a group of people who meet to listen and decide something together. This gate opens only for an honest answer to one question: what changed after contact?

When I drew a map for my cousin to find my house, I put on the street, the big oak tree on the corner, and an arrow pointing north. Every piece told her something. Old mapmakers did the same thing. As you place each piece, ask yourself: what does this piece tell a historian?

Look at your finished card. It has a ship, a route, and a name for the land. Now pause me and count. How many pieces show the people who already lived here? Just one. Keep that question with you on the Explore tab: whose story does a map tell?

Florida is full of names from different people. Okeechobee comes from a Native language. It means big water. St. Augustine is a Spanish name, for a saint. Every name tells you who was there, and who did the naming. Now look at the old map. For each name, ask: who used it first?

Here’s a coin from my own school. Heads: why did we build a new playground? Kids needed more room to play. Tails: what happened to what was already there? A big old tree was cut down, and the birds that lived in it had to find a new home. Both sides are true. Now fill your coin, heads first.
Here’s Antonio de Herrera. He was a Spanish historian, and in 1601 he wrote about Ponce de León’s voyage, using old records of the trip. Listen for the two reasons Ponce chose the name La Florida.

And believing that this land was an island, they named it La Florida, because it had a very beautiful view of many and cool woodlands, and it was level and uniform; and because, moreover, they discovered it in the time of the Feast of Flowers, Juan Ponce wished to conform in the name to these two reasons. He went ashore to get information, and take possession.

Did you catch both reasons? The land was green and full of trees, and it was the Easter season, the Feast of Flowers. Now listen to the last words again: take possession. That means he claimed the land for Spain. Pause me and think: which of the three winds was that?
It’s a card that shows evidence from the past. Old maps are one kind of source. They show what the mapmaker knew, and what they didn’t.
You did it! This file is finished.
Europeans wrote every name on that map. Some names came from Native people, but they were spelled the way Europeans heard them.
Bye! Don’t forget to copy or download your work and turn it in on Canvas. I’ll text you from the next room.
I’m okay! It’s dusty in here, but the maps are beautiful. Let’s keep going.
Go to the Self-Check tab (tab 3). Three quick questions. They aren’t graded.

Now for the writing. In the Historian’s Notebook tab (tab 4), answer three questions. Then write 3 to 5 sentences about why Europeans came, and what happened to the people already here. Fill both sides of the coin first.
Nice work! You read both sides of the story and sorted every name. Next is the Self-Check tab (tab 3).
Because Florida wasn’t empty. People already lived here, in towns along the coasts and rivers.
Tap a piece, then tap its faint outline on the card. Or drag it. Put the coastline on first.
Go to the Explore tab (tab 2). Raise the sail and catch three winds. Each wind is one reason Europeans sailed here.
You did it! Your source card is finished. Look at what it shows about the explorers, and what it shows about the people already here. Next is the Explore tab (tab 2).
Start in the Source Card tab (tab 1). Scroll down to the old map card under the welcome video.
Where do you want to start?
The next file is about St. Augustine. Spain started it in 1565, and people still live there today.
The first file in here is about why Europeans sailed to Florida, and who was already living here when they came.

When I was a kid, a storm once knocked out all the power on my street. For the first time, it was really dark, and really quiet. In 1942, Florida towns turned their own lights off on purpose, because the war had come close. Tap each light to turn it off, and watch the sea.

Pause me for a second. Look out at the water. That glow is a ship on fire. In 1942, enemy submarines sank ships right off Florida, close enough to see from the beach. Say one word out loud for how that would feel. Then go to the Explore tab, tab 2.

That fire really happened, on April 10, 1942. The U.S. Navy kept a war diary, a record of every attack, hour by hour. Here are two real lines from that night. Sub means submarine, and a tanker is a ship that carries oil.
Coast Guard Jacksonville Beach saw sub shelling ship. Bomber pilots reported large explosion same place. S.S. Gulf America, U.S. tanker, torpedoed approximately eight miles south St. John's Light.
Notice how short those lines are. No feelings, just facts. St. John's Light marked the mouth of the St. Johns River, near Jacksonville. People standing on the beach could see this ship burn.
